items.prompt: A reviewer reads a design doc in two minutes and leaves a single comment: 'LGTM.' What failure mode is this, and what does it skip?
choices: Nitpicking — it skips the doc's formatting
Rubber-stamping — it skips testing the design against any real risk
This is a correct, efficient review
Blocking feedback — it skips nothing
items.explanation: Approving without engaging with the design's actual claims is rubber-stamping — it feels efficient and trusting, but it leaves every real risk (scale, failure modes, reversibility) completely unexamined.
items.reference:
Rubber-stamp

Approves without testing anything

Nitpick

Tests only naming/formatting, never the design

Why: both avoid the same hard work — forming a real opinion about whether this design holds up — from opposite directions.

items.prompt: A reviewer leaves 11 comments on a design doc, 9 of them about heading capitalization and variable naming. What failure mode is this?
choices: Rubber-stamping, since no design content was approved outright
Nitpicking — engaging with the doc, but only the cheap, safe parts, never the actual design decisions
This is thorough, rigorous review
Blocking feedback
items.explanation: Volume of comments isn't the same as substance. Nitpicking looks rigorous — look how many comments! — while carefully avoiding the parts of the design that actually carry risk.
items.reference:
Rubber-stamp

Approves without testing anything

Nitpick

Tests only naming/formatting, never the design

Why: both avoid the same hard work — forming a real opinion about whether this design holds up — from opposite directions.

items.prompt: What is a design review actually for, per the unit's framing?
choices: To test the author's competence
To catch decisions that are expensive to reverse later, while they're still cheap to change on paper
To enforce the reviewer's personal formatting preferences
To demonstrate how much the reviewer knows
items.explanation: Review exists because a doc is the cheapest point in a system's whole lifecycle to be wrong at — catching an expensive-to-reverse decision here costs an edit, not a rewrite or a migration.
items.reference:
📄 Doc stage: cheap to change
→
🏗️ Built stage: expensive to change

Why: review's whole value is catching the expensive-to-reverse decision at the cheap-to-change moment.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT a legitimate purpose of a design review, per the unit?
choices: Surfacing risks while they're still cheap to fix
Testing the design against scale, failure, and reversibility concerns
Giving the reviewer a chance to show off technical knowledge unrelated to whether the design holds up
Catching decisions that would be costly to undo after implementation
items.explanation: A review that exists to showcase the reviewer's knowledge, rather than to test the specific design in front of them, has drifted from the actual purpose — the doc's own risks are the point, not the reviewer's résumé.
items.reference:
📄 Doc stage: cheap to change
→
🏗️ Built stage: expensive to change

Why: review's whole value is catching the expensive-to-reverse decision at the cheap-to-change moment.

items.prompt: A reviewer asks: 'What happens to requests if this specific component goes down?' Which of the five question categories does this belong to?
choices: Scale & load
Failure modes & blast radius
Trade-offs & alternatives
Operability & ownership
items.explanation: Asking what happens when a component is down or slow, and how far that failure spreads, is exactly the failure modes & blast radius category — it protects against outages spreading further than planned.
items.reference:
CategoryQuestion
Scale & loadHolds up at 10x? At 1/10th?
Failure & blast radiusWhat happens when this is down?
Trade-offsWhat else was considered?
ReversibilityHow hard to undo in 6 months?
OperabilityWho gets paged, can they debug it?

items.prompt: A reviewer asks: 'Who gets paged when this breaks, and can they actually debug it without the author?' Which category does this belong to?
choices: Reversibility & cost of being wrong
Operability & ownership
Scale & load
Trade-offs & alternatives
items.explanation: Asking who owns and can operate a system after it ships is the operability & ownership category — it protects against systems only the original author can debug.
items.reference:
CategoryQuestion
Scale & loadHolds up at 10x? At 1/10th?
Failure & blast radiusWhat happens when this is down?
Trade-offsWhat else was considered?
ReversibilityHow hard to undo in 6 months?
OperabilityWho gets paged, can they debug it?

items.prompt: A reviewer asks: 'Why was a message queue chosen over just polling the database every few seconds?' Which category does this belong to?
choices: Trade-offs & alternatives
Operability & ownership
Failure modes & blast radius
Scale & load
items.explanation: Asking what else was considered, and why this option won, is the trade-offs & alternatives category — it protects against decisions nobody actually compared to any alternative.
items.reference:
CategoryQuestion
Scale & loadHolds up at 10x? At 1/10th?
Failure & blast radiusWhat happens when this is down?
Trade-offsWhat else was considered?
ReversibilityHow hard to undo in 6 months?
OperabilityWho gets paged, can they debug it?

items.prompt: A reviewer comments: 'This variable should be named `message` instead of `msg`.' What severity level does this belong to, and how should it be labeled?
choices: Blocking — naming matters for maintainability
Should-fix, treated with the same urgency as a missing failure-mode analysis
Nit — a costless-to-skip preference, labeled optional
Question — the reviewer should ask why `msg` was chosen
items.explanation: A naming preference costs nothing to skip and doesn't change whether the design is safe, cheap, or reliable — it belongs in the nit bucket, explicitly labeled optional so it doesn't compete for attention with real findings.
items.reference:
Blocking — real risk, must resolve
Should-fix — improves the design, not a blocker
Question — reviewer genuinely doesn't know
Nit — preference, optional, costs nothing to skip

Why: sorting feedback by what it actually requires keeps a nit from reading with the same weight as a real risk.

items.prompt: A reviewer comments: 'The doc doesn't say what happens if this component is down for an hour — that needs to be answered before this ships.' What severity is this?
choices: Nit
Question
Blocking
Should-fix
items.explanation: This identifies a real, unaddressed risk (a failure mode) and states it must be resolved before the design moves forward — that's the definition of blocking, not a preference or an open-ended question.
items.reference:
Blocking — real risk, must resolve
Should-fix — improves the design, not a blocker
Question — reviewer genuinely doesn't know
Nit — preference, optional, costs nothing to skip

Why: sorting feedback by what it actually requires keeps a nit from reading with the same weight as a real risk.

items.prompt: A reviewer comments: 'I'm not sure what happens if two of these events arrive out of order — can you clarify?' What severity is this, given the reviewer doesn't yet know if it's a real problem?
choices: Blocking
Question — the reviewer genuinely doesn't know the answer and the doc should say
Nit
Should-fix
items.explanation: This isn't a criticism or a demand — it's a genuine unknown the reviewer needs answered. Treating every unknown as an automatic blocker is part of how nitpicking inflates urgency; a real question stays a question until the answer reveals whether it's actually a risk.
items.reference:
Blocking — real risk, must resolve
Should-fix — improves the design, not a blocker
Question — reviewer genuinely doesn't know
Nit — preference, optional, costs nothing to skip

Why: sorting feedback by what it actually requires keeps a nit from reading with the same weight as a real risk.

items.prompt: What test does the unit propose for checking whether a review actually did its job?
choices: Whether the reviewer left more than 5 comments
If every comment on the review were addressed, would the design actually be safer, cheaper, or more reliable?
Whether the meeting ran the full allotted time
Whether the author felt criticized
items.explanation: This test cuts through both failure modes: a rubber-stamped review fails it because there's nothing to address, and a nitpicked review fails it because addressing every comment (all naming and formatting) wouldn't change the design's actual safety or cost at all.
items.reference:
Test: if every comment were addressed, would the design actually be safer, cheaper, or more reliable?

Why: comment count and approval speed both feel like signals of a good review, but neither one is what the test actually checks.

items.prompt: Using the unit's test ('if every comment were addressed, would the design be safer, cheaper, or more reliable?'), why does a review with 9 naming comments and 2 'LGTM's fail it, even though 11 comments sounds thorough?
choices: It doesn't fail — 11 comments is objectively thorough
Because addressing every naming comment wouldn't change the design's safety, cost, or reliability at all — the volume is real, the substance isn't
Because 11 comments is too many for a 45-minute review window
Because 'LGTM' comments should be removed entirely
items.explanation: The test isn't about how many comments exist — it's about whether addressing them changes anything real about the design. Nine formatting fixes and two approvals leave every actual risk in the doc exactly as unexamined as a review with zero comments.
items.reference:
Test: if every comment were addressed, would the design actually be safer, cheaper, or more reliable?

Why: comment count and approval speed both feel like signals of a good review, but neither one is what the test actually checks.

items.prompt: The unit argues rubber-stamping and nitpicking are both ways of avoiding the same harder work. What is that harder work?
choices: Writing more comments than the other reviewers
Forming a real opinion about whether this specific design will hold up, and saying so
Memorizing every architecture pattern in advance
Making the meeting finish on time
items.explanation: Rubber-stamping skips the hard work by not looking closely enough to form an opinion; nitpicking skips it by looking closely at everything except the parts that would require forming one. Both end up avoiding the same commitment: a real, stated judgment about the design itself.
items.reference:
Rubber-stamp: avoids by not looking.
Nitpick: avoids by looking at everything except what matters.

Why: both dodge the one thing a review is actually for — a real, stated opinion on whether the design holds up.

items.prompt: Per the unit's review flow, what should a reviewer do before leaving any comments at all?
choices: Comment on issues as soon as they're spotted, to avoid forgetting them
Read the whole doc once, fully, to form an opinion about the design as a whole
Ask the author to summarize the doc out loud first
Sort existing team feedback by whoever commented first
items.explanation: Commenting mid-read locks a reviewer into reacting to whatever is in front of them, which is usually surface-level — naming, phrasing — because that's what's cheap to notice on a first pass. Reading fully first forces a real opinion about the whole design before reacting to any one sentence.
items.reference:
Flow: read fully → list claims → test against categories → sort by severity → deliver blocking first

Why: commenting while still reading is exactly how nitpicking starts — the easiest things to react to mid-read are surface details, not the design's real claims.

items.prompt: A reviewer leaves a comment on paragraph two questioning phrasing before reading the rest of the 18-page doc. What's the specific risk this creates, per the unit's flow?
choices: None — early comments save time later
The reviewer spends their attention on cheap, surface-level details before reaching the doc's actual load-bearing claims, which often appear later
It guarantees the review will be too short
It automatically counts as rubber-stamping
items.explanation: The doc's real claims about failure modes and scale often don't show up until later sections. A reviewer who's already deep into phrasing comments by paragraph two has spent their attention before reaching the parts most worth spending it on.
items.reference:
Flow: read fully → list claims → test against categories → sort by severity → deliver blocking first

Why: commenting while still reading is exactly how nitpicking starts — the easiest things to react to mid-read are surface details, not the design's real claims.

items.prompt: Per the unit's cost-of-change chart, at what stage is changing a design decision cheapest?
choices: In production, once real usage patterns are known
Mid-implementation, once code exists to guide the change
At the doc review stage, before code or infrastructure exists
Cost is the same at every stage
items.explanation: Changing a decision in a doc is an edit to a page. The same change mid-implementation means rewriting code already built around the wrong assumption; in production, it's a migration. Cost climbs sharply the later a flaw is caught.
items.reference:
Relative cost to change: doc review ≈2 → prototype ≈12 → mid-implementation ≈45 → production ≈100

Why: review's economic case rests entirely on catching flaws at the cheapest possible point in the lifecycle.

items.prompt: Using the unit's cost-of-change chart, why does the relative cost jump so much more between 'mid-implementation' and 'in production' than between 'doc review' and 'prototype'?
choices: It doesn't — the chart shows a flat, linear increase throughout
Because production changes require a migration with a rollback plan, affecting real traffic and data, not just unfinished code
Because prototypes are always more expensive than production systems
Because doc review takes longer than implementation
items.explanation: Early-stage changes touch only plans or unfinished code — nothing is depending on them yet. A production change has to happen without breaking whatever is already running on the old assumption, which is why the cost curve steepens sharply at that stage rather than growing evenly.
items.reference:
Relative cost to change: doc review ≈2 → prototype ≈12 → mid-implementation ≈45 → production ≈100

Why: review's economic case rests entirely on catching flaws at the cheapest possible point in the lifecycle.

items.prompt: A team says 'we'll skip the design review and just fix issues during code review instead.' Using the cost-of-change chart, what's the flaw in that plan?
choices: There's no flaw — code review catches the same issues at the same cost
Code review happens after implementation has already started, so the same flaw now costs a rewrite instead of a page edit
Code review is always slower than design review
Design review and code review test identical things, so skipping one is redundant
items.explanation: Code review happens at the mid-implementation stage on the chart, well past the cheapest point. A design flaw caught there means code already built around the wrong shape has to be reworked — the same flaw, caught later, for a much higher cost.
items.reference:
Relative cost to change: doc review ≈2 → prototype ≈12 → mid-implementation ≈45 → production ≈100

Why: review's economic case rests entirely on catching flaws at the cheapest possible point in the lifecycle.

items.prompt: The unit uses the same five question categories on every doc, regardless of what the doc happens to emphasize. Why a fixed set, rather than letting each doc's own structure guide what gets asked?
choices: A fixed set is arbitrary and doesn't matter which categories are used
Letting the doc's own structure guide the review lets the author's framing decide what gets scrutinized, which is exactly how a doc's blind spots stay unexamined
Fixed categories are only needed for very long docs
The categories change every time based on the reviewer's mood
items.explanation: If a review only reacts to whatever the doc chooses to emphasize, then whatever the author didn't think to mention — the actual blind spot — never gets tested either, since nothing in the doc prompts a question about it. A fixed, external checklist is what catches the doc's own gaps, not just its stated claims.
items.reference:
CategoryQuestion
Scale & loadHolds up at 10x? At 1/10th?
Failure & blast radiusWhat happens when this is down?
Trade-offsWhat else was considered?
ReversibilityHow hard to undo in 6 months?
OperabilityWho gets paged, can they debug it?

Why: a doc can only prompt questions about what it already mentions — a fixed checklist is what reaches the parts it left out.

items.prompt: Per the unit's rigor/tone matrix, what combination produces rubber-stamping?
choices: High rigor, collaborative tone
Low rigor, collaborative tone
High rigor, adversarial tone
Low rigor, adversarial tone
items.explanation: Rubber-stamping sits at low rigor, collaborative tone — friendly, but nothing about the design actually gets tested.
items.reference:
Low rigor + collaborative
Rubber-stamp
High rigor + collaborative
Target
Low rigor + adversarial
Nitpick as toughness
High rigor + adversarial
Correct but ignored

items.prompt: A reviewer asks exactly the right questions from all five categories but phrases every one as a judgment on the author's competence. Per the matrix, what outcome does this predict?
choices: The design gets fixed quickly since the findings are correct
High rigor, adversarial tone — technically correct findings, but the author gets defensive and the feedback is likely to be ignored or resisted
This automatically counts as rubber-stamping
The matrix predicts no difference from a collaborative version
items.explanation: Rigor gets a reviewer to the right questions; tone determines whether the author can hear them. Correct findings delivered adversarially predict a defensive author, which tends to slow down resolution even though the content was right.
items.reference:
Low rigor + collaborative
Rubber-stamp
High rigor + collaborative
Target
Low rigor + adversarial
Nitpick as toughness
High rigor + adversarial
Correct but ignored

items.prompt: A reviewer leaves many harshly-worded comments but none of them test the design's actual scale, failure modes, or trade-offs. Where does this land on the matrix?
choices: High rigor, collaborative tone
Low rigor, adversarial tone — nitpicking dressed up as toughness
High rigor, adversarial tone
This is the matrix's target cell
items.explanation: Volume and harshness aren't rigor — rigor means actually testing the design's claims. Many harsh comments that never touch the real risk categories is nitpicking wearing the costume of thoroughness, not the substance of it.
items.reference:
Low rigor + collaborative
Rubber-stamp
High rigor + collaborative
Target
Low rigor + adversarial
Nitpick as toughness
High rigor + adversarial
Correct but ignored

items.prompt: Per the unit's flow, once findings are sorted by severity, in what order should they be delivered?
choices: Nits first, to warm up the conversation before harder topics
In the order they were noticed while reading
Blocking items first, with nits delivered last and clearly labeled optional
Randomly, so nothing seems prioritized over anything else
items.explanation: Delivering blocking items first keeps the author's attention on what actually has to change before anything else; nits delivered last and labeled optional keep them from competing with real findings for attention.
items.reference:
Flow: read fully → list claims → test against categories → sort by severity → deliver blocking first

Why: delivery order signals urgency — burying a blocking issue among nits makes it easy to miss.

items.prompt: A reviewer delivers 9 naming nits first, then mentions a missing failure-mode analysis as the last of 11 comments. What's the practical risk of this ordering, even though the finding itself is correct?
choices: None, order doesn't affect how feedback is received
The genuinely blocking finding is easy for the author to miss or deprioritize, buried among comments that don't matter
It automatically makes the comment count as a nit instead of blocking
It guarantees the author will reject all the feedback
items.explanation: Order carries information about urgency whether or not the reviewer intends it to. Burying the one real risk at the end of a long list of nits makes it easy for the author to treat it with the same low priority as everything around it.
items.reference:
Flow: read fully → list claims → test against categories → sort by severity → deliver blocking first

Why: delivery order signals urgency — burying a blocking issue among nits makes it easy to miss.

items.prompt: Per the unit's flow, what comes right after reading the doc fully, before any severity sorting happens?
choices: Listing the design's load-bearing claims, then testing each one against the five question categories
Immediately approving or rejecting the doc
Scheduling a follow-up meeting
Rewriting the doc's formatting
items.explanation: After a full read, the flow moves to identifying the doc's actual claims (what it asserts will be true) and testing each one against the five categories — this is the step that turns a read-through into a substantive review, before anything gets sorted by severity.
items.reference:
Flow: read fully → list claims → test against categories → sort by severity → deliver blocking first

Why: testing claims against fixed categories is what keeps a review from just reacting to whatever catches the eye.

items.prompt: What is a design's 'load-bearing claim,' in the sense the unit's flow uses the term?
choices: Any sentence that uses architecture jargon
A statement the design's correctness or safety actually depends on — something that would matter if it turned out to be false
The longest paragraph in the doc
Any claim the author personally feels strongly about
items.explanation: A load-bearing claim is one the design leans on — if it turns out false or incomplete (like 'no orders are lost' quietly meaning only 'no bytes are lost'), something real about the system's correctness or safety is at stake. Listing these before testing them is what separates a substantive review from reacting to whatever sentence is easiest to comment on.
items.reference:
Flow: read fully → list claims → test against categories → sort by severity → deliver blocking first

Why: testing claims against fixed categories is what keeps a review from just reacting to whatever catches the eye.

items.prompt: The doc says: 'This removes the latency from the checkout path entirely.' Reading just this claim, what's the most useful next question for a reviewer to hold onto (not necessarily ask yet)?
choices: Whether the sentence is grammatically correct
What happens to a notification after it's published — the claim is true for the checkout path, but says nothing about delivery afterward
Whether Kafka is the correct product name to use
Whether the 180ms number should be rounded differently
items.explanation: The claim is narrowly true (checkout no longer waits), but it doesn't address what happens to the notification once decoupled — that's a genuine gap worth holding onto while reading the rest of the doc, per the unit's flow of reading fully before reacting.
items.reference:
Doc claims tested against the 5 categories: 'removes latency entirely' (scope), 'no orders lost' (durability vs. correctness), 'drop-in replacement' (operability).

Why: a claim can be true and still incomplete — testing it against a category is what surfaces the gap a fast read would miss.

items.prompt: The doc says: 'Kafka retains events for 7 days, so no orders are lost.' Which category does testing this claim most directly belong to, and why?
choices: Reversibility & cost of being wrong — 'no orders lost' conflates message durability with correct processing, and duplicate or dropped processing is a real cost if wrong
Scale & load — the claim is really about topic size
Trade-offs & alternatives — the claim compares Kafka to other message brokers
This claim doesn't need testing since 7-day retention is a Kafka default
items.explanation: The claim bundles two different guarantees (message durability vs. correct-once processing) under one reassuring phrase. Testing it means asking what the actual delivery guarantee is and what happens if processing happens twice — a reversibility/cost-of-being-wrong question, not a scale or trade-off one.
items.reference:
Doc claims tested against the 5 categories: 'removes latency entirely' (scope), 'no orders lost' (durability vs. correctness), 'drop-in replacement' (operability).

Why: a claim can be true and still incomplete — testing it against a category is what surfaces the gap a fast read would miss.

items.prompt: The doc says: 'This is a drop-in replacement... single deploy, cut over, done.' What does this claim skip, per the categories it should be tested against?
choices: Nothing — it's a complete rollout plan
A rollback plan if the new consumer has a bug post-cutover, and what happens to orders already in flight mid-deploy (operability & ownership)
The exact Kafka version being used
Whether the deploy happens on a Friday
items.explanation: 'Single deploy, cut over, done' skips two operability questions: how to recover if something goes wrong after cutover, and what happens to in-flight orders during the transition. Neither is addressed, which is exactly the gap the operability & ownership category is built to surface.
items.reference:
Doc claims tested against the 5 categories: 'removes latency entirely' (scope), 'no orders lost' (durability vs. correctness), 'drop-in replacement' (operability).

Why: a claim can be true and still incomplete — testing it against a category is what surfaces the gap a fast read would miss.

items.prompt: In the worked review, 'no poison-pill handling described' for the notification consumer was sorted as blocking. Why blocking rather than should-fix?
choices: Because it's about naming
Because without it, one bad event could silently stall all order confirmations behind it — a real, unaddressed risk to the system working at all
Because the reviewer personally dislikes the design
All findings in a review should default to blocking
items.explanation: A missing dead-letter/retry-cap strategy isn't a nice-to-have — without it, a single malformed event can block or infinitely retry, stalling everything behind it in the queue. That's a real risk to correctness, which is what makes it blocking rather than should-fix.
items.reference:
BlockingPoison-pill handling; delivery-guarantee/idempotency
Should-fixRollback plan; expected volume/partitioning
QuestionWhy Kafka over a simpler queue?
NitInconsistent 'OrderService' capitalization

items.prompt: In the worked review, 'no stated rollback plan for the cutover' was sorted as should-fix rather than blocking. What distinguishes it from the poison-pill finding, which was blocking?
choices: It doesn't threaten correctness the way an unhandled poison-pill message does — it's a real operational gap worth closing, but not one that stalls the system outright
Should-fix findings are always less important than the reviewer's opinion
There is no real distinction; this was miscategorized
Rollback plans are never actually necessary
items.explanation: The two findings differ in what's actually at stake: an unhandled poison-pill message can silently stall the whole system, which is a correctness risk. A missing rollback plan is a real operational gap — worth fixing before shipping — but the system can still function correctly without one; it's riskier to operate, not incorrect by design.
items.reference:
BlockingPoison-pill handling; delivery-guarantee/idempotency
Should-fixRollback plan; expected volume/partitioning
QuestionWhy Kafka over a simpler queue?
NitInconsistent 'OrderService' capitalization

items.prompt: 'Was a simpler background job queue considered before Kafka specifically?' was sorted as a question rather than blocking or should-fix. Why?
choices: Because the reviewer already knows the answer is no
Because the reviewer isn't asserting the choice is wrong — they genuinely don't know the reasoning yet, and the doc should record it for future readers
Because trade-off comments are never worth asking
Because it's really a nit about wording
items.explanation: This comment doesn't claim Kafka is the wrong choice — it asks for the reasoning to be made explicit, which may already exist just not be written down. That open, non-accusatory framing is exactly what keeps it a question rather than an assumed blocking objection.
items.reference:
BlockingPoison-pill handling; delivery-guarantee/idempotency
Should-fixRollback plan; expected volume/partitioning
QuestionWhy Kafka over a simpler queue?
NitInconsistent 'OrderService' capitalization

items.prompt: The doc states 'each event is processed independently,' with no mention of retry limits or a dead-letter topic. What's the specific risk this leaves open?
choices: None — 'processed independently' already guarantees isolation between events
One event that keeps failing to process (a poison pill) could retry forever or block the events behind it, stalling confirmations for unrelated orders
The risk only applies if Kafka itself goes down
This only matters if the notification service has a memory leak
items.explanation: 'Processed independently' describes intent, not a mechanism — without a stated retry cap or dead-letter topic, nothing in the doc actually prevents one malformed event from consuming retries indefinitely or blocking the events queued behind it, regardless of how independent the processing is meant to be.
items.reference:
No retry cap / dead-letter topic stated → one bad event can block or infinitely retry, stalling everything behind it.

Why: 'processed independently' describes the goal, not a guarantee — the doc needs a mechanism, not just an intention.

items.prompt: Why does the unit sort the missing poison-pill handling as blocking rather than a nice-to-have suggestion for later?
choices: Because it's a formatting concern
Because without it, the system has no defined behavior for a realistic failure case, and the failure could silently degrade the entire notification pipeline
Because all failure-mode comments are automatically blocking regardless of impact
Because the author asked for it to be marked blocking
items.explanation: This isn't a hypothetical edge case — malformed or unprocessable events are a realistic occurrence in any event-driven system, and leaving the behavior undefined risks a single bad event quietly degrading the whole pipeline. That combination (realistic, undefined, systemic impact) is what makes it blocking rather than a should-fix.
items.reference:
No retry cap / dead-letter topic stated → one bad event can block or infinitely retry, stalling everything behind it.

Why: 'processed independently' describes the goal, not a guarantee — the doc needs a mechanism, not just an intention.

items.prompt: If the notification consumer uses at-least-once delivery (Kafka's common default) and isn't idempotent, what's the realistic customer-facing consequence?
choices: No consequence — at-least-once delivery guarantees exactly one send
A customer could receive a duplicate confirmation email or SMS if the same event gets reprocessed
The order itself could be silently cancelled
The customer would never receive any confirmation at all
items.explanation: At-least-once delivery guarantees a message is delivered one or more times, not exactly once — if the consumer doesn't dedupe or check idempotency before sending, a reprocessed event sends a second confirmation to the same customer.
items.reference:
At-least-once delivery + non-idempotent send → possible duplicate customer-facing notification.

Why: 'no orders lost' (durability) and 'sent exactly once' (correctness) are different guarantees that a doc can easily blur together.

items.prompt: Why does the unit treat the missing idempotency detail as blocking for this doc, even though a duplicate email is a minor annoyance?
choices: Because any undefined behavior is automatically blocking regardless of impact
Because the doc's own claim ('no orders are lost') implies a stronger guarantee than it actually provides, and the gap should be named explicitly rather than left to be discovered in production
Because duplicate emails always cause serious financial harm
It shouldn't be blocking — the unit is wrong to sort it that way
items.explanation: The severity comes from the doc overstating its own guarantee, not just the size of the consequence — 'no orders are lost' reads as a completeness claim, but the actual behavior (possible duplicate sends) isn't described anywhere. Making that explicit before shipping is exactly the kind of gap that's cheap to fix in a doc and easy to miss once it's live.
items.reference:
At-least-once delivery + non-idempotent send → possible duplicate customer-facing notification.

Why: 'no orders lost' (durability) and 'sent exactly once' (correctness) are different guarantees that a doc can easily blur together.

items.prompt: Comparing 'There's no error handling here at all, this would fall over immediately in production' vs. 'What happens if a specific event fails to process — does it retry forever, get skipped, or block the ones behind it?' — both flag the same real gap. What's the functional difference?
choices: There is no functional difference, they're equally effective
The first states a verdict about the design (and implicitly the author); the second asks a specific, answerable question the author can act on directly
The second comment fails to identify a blocking issue
The first comment is more technically accurate
items.explanation: Both identify the same blocking gap correctly — the difference is entirely in delivery. The first frames it as a judgment ('this would fall over,' implicitly 'you missed this'), while the second asks a concrete question the author can answer or act on without first having to manage how the comment made them feel.
items.reference:
Adversarial: 'No error handling at all, this would fall over.'
Collaborative: 'What happens if an event fails to process — retry, skip, or block?'

Why: same finding, same rigor — tone decides whether the author can hear it without first managing how it feels.

items.prompt: Someone argues the adversarial phrasing ('no error handling at all... falls over immediately') is more efficient because it's shorter. Why is that efficiency likely false, per the unit?
choices: Because shorter comments are always factually wrong

Because the variable that determines speed to a fixed design is the author's ability to engage, and a defensive response tends to produce a slower back-and-forth than a specific, actionable question would
Because longer comments are required by the review tool
It isn't false — the shorter version really is faster
items.explanation: Comment length isn't what determines how fast a design actually gets fixed — the author's ability to act on the feedback without managing defensiveness first is. A blunt verdict predicts a slower resolution (clarifying the tone, or a narrow literal fix) than a specific question the author can act on immediately.
items.reference:
Adversarial: 'No error handling at all, this would fall over.'
Collaborative: 'What happens if an event fails to process — retry, skip, or block?'

Why: same finding, same rigor — tone decides whether the author can hear it without first managing how it feels.

items.prompt: The same design pattern (Kafka, at-least-once delivery, no stated idempotency) is proposed for a payment-confirmation event instead of order notifications, where a duplicate delivery risks charging a customer twice. What changes about the review?
choices: Nothing changes — severity should be identical regardless of what the event represents
The idempotency gap moves from 'should clarify' territory toward unambiguously blocking, since the cost of the same technical gap is now a financial error instead of an annoying duplicate email
The doc would no longer need a design review at all
Kafka would no longer be an appropriate choice under any circumstances
items.explanation: The technical gap is identical — the same at-least-once delivery risk. What changes is the cost of being wrong: a duplicate email is a minor annoyance, a duplicate charge is a real financial and trust problem. Severity isn't just about the size of the technical gap; it scales with what's actually at stake if it goes wrong, which is why the same finding can be should-fix in one context and blocking in another.
items.reference:
Same technical gap, different stakes: notifications vs. payments. Same categories, different setting: private doc vs. public meeting.

Why: the categories and severity logic don't bend for context — but what counts as blocking, and how a finding should be phrased, both track what's actually at stake.

items.prompt: If the same design were presented by the team's most senior architect in a live meeting instead of a first-time author's written doc, what would the unit's framework suggest should change about how comments are phrased?
choices: Rigor should drop, since a senior architect is unlikely to have made a real mistake

The five categories and severity sorting stay the same — a real gap is a real gap regardless of seniority — but tone may need more care in a live, public setting, where a comment lands in front of a room rather than privately in a doc
Nothing about delivery should change; seniority is irrelevant to tone
Only nits should be raised, since senior architects should not receive blocking feedback
items.explanation: The categories and severity sorting don't bend for seniority — a poison-pill gap is exactly as real regardless of who wrote the design. What can reasonably change is the setting's effect on tone: a live, public correction carries a different social cost than a private doc comment, which argues for even more deliberate, question-first phrasing, not for lowering rigor or withholding a real finding.
